languages.verdict: Good fit, and the best non-C source for Phase 1. Fat-LTO staticlib bitcode from rustc 1.99 (LLVM 23.1.1) has run end to end on this machine. With the uncommitted M9 changes, core::fmt through dyn Write also works. panic=abort removes unwinding, and Rust has no GC. The remaining gaps are aliases from function merging, user-written u128 division, atomics in alloc/sync types, black_box and memcmp.
languages.integration_path: rustc --edition 2021 --crate-type staticlib -C panic=abort -C opt-level=2 -C lto=fat -C codegen-units=1 -C llvm-args=-mergefunc-use-aliases=false --emit=llvm-bc,link --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc. For the Linux layout use x86_64-unknown-none: it has the same data-layout string as x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, but a softfloat rustc-abi and the kernel code model (extern 'C' floats are still double in the IR). The `link` part is required, because without it core and alloc stay as declarations. With it, the result is one post-LTO module whose only non-intrinsic declarations are the imports (verified). The mergefunc flag makes identical functions thunks instead of aliases, which MSIL rejects (the nightly alternative is -Zmerge-functions=disabled). Next, run opt -passes=lower-atomic if Arc, AtomicUsize or spin locks are present (verified for Arc). Then llc -O2 -mtriple=<native>-msil, ilasm and dotnet. Program shape: #![no_std] #![no_main], #[no_mangle] extern 'C' fn main() -> i32, a #[panic_handler] that calls puts and loops or traps, a bump #[global_allocator] over a static array, and output through extern 'C' putchar/puts. Later options: a custom target JSON with the msil triple (-Zbuild-std=core,alloc, nightly); in Phase 2, -Clinker-plugin-lto with msil-ld; in Phase 3, real std with panic=abort.
languages.earliest_phase: Phase 1 for no_std plus alloc. core::fmt works once M9 is committed (verified on the uncommitted M9 tree). Phase 3 for std.
languages.blockers:
- Unwinding: never. panic=abort is mandatory, so catch_unwind and should_panic tests are permanently out, and under libtest the first failure ends the process. Functions keep `personality @__CxxFrameHandler3` with no EH pads, and llc-msil accepts that on both triples (verified).
- GC root finding: not applicable.
- Aliases: rustc -O emits `unnamed_addr alias` for identical functions, and MSIL rejects every GlobalAlias. -C llvm-args=-mergefunc-use-aliases=false fixes this (verified).
- u128: user-written `/` and `%` by a non-power-of-two, and float-to-u128 casts, become __udivti3/__fixunsdfti. The backend reports these as Phase-3 helpers even when they are defined, and compiler_builtins is not in the LTO module (verified). Formatting u128 works, because core::fmt uses mul i128 (verified). Suggested fix: in MSIL lowering, setMaxDivRemBitWidthSupported(64) and setMaxLargeFPConvertBitWidthSupported(64), as NVPTX and AMDGPU do, so ExpandIRInsts expands these inline. i1024 division already expands inline this way.
- black_box: becomes `asm sideeffect "", "r,~{memory}"(ptr)`, which MSILPrepareIR rejects. Suggested fix: accept an empty asm string with inputs and clobbers but no outputs, treat the operand as escaped and the call as a compiler barrier.
- memcmp/bcmp: slice and str comparisons declare memcmp, which is not a Phase-1 import. Define it in Rust or tag it with msil-import-module.
- Atomics: Arc, spin and once_cell become __atomic_* calls (the maximum atomic size is 0). Run lower-atomic (single-threaded only) until Phase 3.
- TLS: none in no_std. std needs thread_local!, real atomics, a futex Mutex and variadic libc, so Phase 3.
- Allocator: user-supplied in Phase 1.
- SIMD and asm: force crates onto their portable backends with cfg flags, because llvm.x86.* intrinsics and cpuid asm break the retarget.

picks.name: Hand-written no_std smoke programs
picks.what: Small self-checking programs: sieve, FNV-1a, u128 shifts and multiplies, Newton sqrt, float math, saturating `as` casts, Box/Vec/BTreeMap/Rc (and Arc via lower-atomic) over a bump allocator, and write! into a dyn core::fmt::Write. Output goes through putchar/puts, and each program ends with a known exit code.
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 (now; core::fmt once M9 is committed)
picks.why_good: Verified end to end: a no_std program with Vec, Rc, a bump allocator, write! into dyn Write (10 indirect calls) and u128 Display printed the expected output on .NET 8 with the M9 llc, and Arc clone/drop ran after lower-atomic. Output is deterministic and is checked against a native build or Python. The programs pin down Rust-specific IR: llvm.fptoui.sat, ucmp, umin/umax, vector.reduce from autovectorization, and a personality with no EH pads.
picks.blockers: Pass -mergefunc-use-aliases=false. Avoid black_box, u128 `/` and `%` by non-powers-of-two, float-to-u128 casts, and slice or str compares without a memcmp definition.
claims_to_verify: The existing Arc/Rc test still exits with 56 after lower-atomic. Arc clone/drop was verified, but that test was not rerun.
x86_64-unknown-none builds (softfloat rustc-abi, kernel code model) run correctly on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-msil, not only compile

picks.name: rustc_codegen_gcc tests/run (plus rustc_codegen_cranelift example/mini_core)
picks.what: 50 backend bring-up programs (array, structs, tuple, closure, fun_ptr, int_overflow, int_intrinsics, float, slice, static, sret, overaligned_byval, packed_u128, switchint_128bit, volatile, ptr_cast, return-tuple, abort, exit_code and others). Many are #![no_core] on mini_core and need no sysroot; int.rs uses std. The expected status and stdout are in each file's `// Run-time:` header. cg_clif's mini_core.rs and mini_core_hello_world.rs, with the TLS, thread and asm parts cut out, complement them.
picks.why_good: The same job as this corpus: a new backend bringing up rustc's IR feature by feature. The oracles are already machine-readable. It covers sret, overaligned byval and 128-bit switches, which are exactly the Phase-1 ABI items.
picks.blockers:
- The no_core tests print through printf, which is variadic (Phase 3). Swap in a putchar-based integer printer in mini_core.
- Excluded: asm.rs and catch_unwind.rs (never).
- atomic_* tests need lower-atomic or Phase 3.
- Weak or import linkage tests need Phase 2.
- int.rs uses std and black_box.
claims_to_verify: Which of the 50 files use std and which use mini_core
Every file, not only int.rs, has a parseable `// Run-time:` header
mini_core.rs compiles with the current stable rustc (lang items may need RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1)
Which tests use u128 division or remainder. These hit the Phase-3 helper error unless the inline expansion fix lands.

picks.name: libm crate (Rust port of musl libm)
picks.what: Pure-Rust sin, cos, exp, log, pow, fma, cbrt, lgamma and friends. crates.io libm 0.2.16 is #![no_std] (development moved to rust-lang/compiler-builtins), so as a dependency every function is defined inside the module. A driver runs exported input and expected-output tables and prints bit patterns.
picks.why_good: A float-codegen test with bit-exact oracles: the same algorithm natively and on MSIL must give identical bits. Its results can be compared with the backend's Phase-1 libm imports. It needs no allocator, atomics or TLS.
picks.blockers: Skip the f16 and f128 functions (CIL has no type for fp128, and f16 helpers are Phase 3). FP-environment functions are not supported.
claims_to_verify: Post-LTO IR of the f32/f64 functions has no `udiv i128`/`urem i128` and no float-to-i128 conversion (grep the .ll)
Expected-value tables can be extracted from libm-test (MPFR/musl based) without running MPFR on the target
The CLR's float32 path keeps f32 results bit-identical, with no double rounding

picks.name: RustCrypto sha2 + chacha20 with ed25519-dalek/curve25519-dalek (portable backends)
picks.what: Hashes, a stream cipher and signatures, all checked against published vectors (NIST SHA, RFC 8439, RFC 8032 and SUPERCOP sign.input). The program prints hex digests and signatures, which are diffed against sha256sum, OpenSSL or the native build.
picks.why_good: Fully deterministic, with authoritative vectors. It is heavy on rotates, wrapping adds and u64×u64→u128 multiply chains, and has large precomputed constant tables (a data-segment stress test). It needs no alloc, atomics or TLS once the portable backends are forced.
picks.blockers:
- The portable backends must be forced: --cfg sha2_backend="soft" (sha2 0.11, or the force-soft feature in 0.10), --cfg chacha20_backend="soft" and --cfg curve25519_dalek_backend="serial".
- Without them, cpufeatures brings in cpuid inline asm and an atomic cache, and the x86 backends bring in llvm.x86.* intrinsics.
- zeroize uses volatile writes and compiler_fence, which should be fine after M7.
claims_to_verify: The exact cfg names and values for the crate versions resolved on the day
The post-LTO IR has no llvm.x86.* calls and no inline asm (grep)
There is no i128 division anywhere in the curve25519 field arithmetic
The precomputed-tables feature's static data assembles under ilasm within size limits
ed25519-dalek with default-features=false still verifies the RFC 8032 vectors without alloc

picks.name: wasmi WebAssembly interpreter with the official spec testsuite
picks.what: wasmi built with default-features=false and libm. The program feeds it .wasm modules and assertion lists precompiled on the host (each .wast converted to a .wasm plus an expected-results table) from static arrays, and prints pass or fail for each assertion.
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 after M9 (with lower-atomic). Phase 3 with real atomics.
picks.why_good: Huge dispatch loops and jump tables; both portable and indirect dispatch can be built, which stresses calli tables. It exercises exact i32/i64/f32/f64 semantics and saturating conversions. The spec testsuite holds tens of thousands of deterministic assertions, and wasmi claims 100% compliance natively, so any failure is a backend bug.
picks.blockers:
- spin and Arc require lower-atomic.
- Needs an allocator.
- Error paths use fmt (M9).
- The .wast runner needs std, so assertions must be generated on the host.
- NaN-payload assertions depend on how the CLR treats float32 NaNs.
claims_to_verify: wasmi's no_std build pulls in only spin plus Arc, and lower-atomic turns all of them into plain loads and stores
The CLR preserves signaling-NaN payloads through float32 ldind/stind and bitcasts (the wasm spec tests check NaN bits); otherwise those assertions must be split out
There is a practical host-side tool that turns .wast into binary modules plus an expected-results table (for example wabt's wast2json)
The resulting module stays within ilasm and CLR method-size limits (one huge dispatch function)

picks.name: rust-lang/rust library/coretests and library/alloctests
picks.what: The unit tests for core and alloc, run with a custom single-process harness, or with libtest one test per process under panic=abort.
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 3 (libtest needs std). A no_std harness is possible after M9 but costly.
picks.why_good: Thousands of focused tests with a published .NET comparison point: rustc_codegen_clr reports 1764 of 1832 core tests passing (96.29%) and 92.77% of alloc tests. This is the conformance yardstick for Phase 4.
picks.blockers:
- libtest needs std, which means TLS, atomics, threads and variadic libc.
- should_panic and catch_unwind tests can never pass and must be filtered out.
- -Zbuild-std is required.
claims_to_verify: coretests and alloctests build with -Zbuild-std and -Cpanic=abort into a fat-LTO staticlib
How many tests carry #[should_panic] or call catch_unwind
Whether the rustc_codegen_clr figures are current, and which of its failures are .NET-specific

languages.verdict: Good fit, and the strongest non-Rust candidate. It has no GC and no unwinding (errors are values), panics go to an overridable handler, and the freestanding target needs no libc. It stresses integer legalization (odd and huge widths), overflow builtins and packed structs harder than C does.
languages.integration_path: zig build-obj (or zig test with a custom --test-runner) -target x86_64-freestanding-none -mcpu=baseline -fsingle-threaded -OReleaseSmall (or ReleaseFast) -femit-llvm-bc=out.bc -fno-emit-bin (flags verified in 0.15.1). Then llc -mtriple=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-msil (or the windows-msvc triple with -target x86_64-windows), ilasm and dotnet. Provide `export fn main() c_int`, an extern putchar, and a root `pub const panic` that is a namespace type (std.debug.FullPanic(myFn), std.debug.simple_panic or std.debug.no_panic), not a bare function. Zig 0.15.1 uses LLVM 20.1.8 but writes bitcode with its own writer (Builder.toBitcode). Non-exported functions are fastcc, which MSIL accepts. llvm.memcpy/memset/memmove become cpblk/Buffer.MemoryCopy/initblk, so only an explicit call to a memcpy symbol would need a definition. A second route is -ofmt=c followed by the fork's clang.
languages.blockers:
- Unwinding: none in the language.
- GC: none.
- TLS: -fsingle-threaded turns threadlocal variables into plain globals (verified in the 0.15.1 source). Without it, MSIL rejects them.
- Atomics: std.atomic is used in std. Avoid it, or run lower-atomic.
- Allocator: explicit by design (FixedBufferAllocator works freestanding).
- Rejected types: fp128 and x86_fp80 (f128, f80, c_longdouble), plus f16 helpers until Phase 3.
- u128 `/` and `%` are Phase-3 helper errors (see the Rust entry for the suggested inline-expansion fix). Integers wider than 128 bits expand inline (verified for i1024).
- std on Linux without libc makes syscalls through inline asm, which is never supported. With libc, start.zig defines main(argc, argv, envp), which emitEntryPoint rejects.
- The default panic handler and test runner pull in std.debug stack traces.
- @Vector tests are SIMD (Phase 4).

picks.name: Hand-written freestanding Zig smoke programs
picks.what: Programs covering odd widths (u3, i65, u1024), @addWithOverflow/@mulWithOverflow, saturating ops, packed structs, error unions and switch on errors, comptime-generated tables, slices and optionals, and function-pointer tables. Each prints through putchar and exits with a code.
picks.why_good: They pin down Zig-specific IR, such as i65 and u1024 arithmetic and packed-struct bitcasts, before the large suite runs. u1024 division is already verified to expand inline. Output is deterministic and comparable with a native zig build.
picks.blockers: Avoid u128 `/` and `%` and f16/f80/f128.
claims_to_verify: The fork's llc reads Zig 0.15.1's self-written bitcode without errors
Code using @memcpy/@memset leaves no explicit call to a memcpy or memset symbol (compiler_rt is normally a separate object)
out.bc contains no GlobalAlias (for example from exporting one decl under several names), since MSIL rejects every alias
picks.size: tens to hundreds of lines each

picks.name: Zig test/behavior with a custom single-threaded test runner
picks.what: The language behavior tests: 2008 in 0.15.1, of which the LLVM backend passes 1977. A custom --test-runner walks builtin.test_functions, calls each one, and prints the name plus ok or fail through putchar. Tests are compiled in groups (with --test-filter) to keep modules small.
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 (needs M9 for the test_functions table)
picks.why_good: Written to be run by several immature backends, so each test is self-contained and has a pass/fail oracle. Wide coverage of integer, float, struct and union, optional, error and comptime codegen.
picks.blockers:
- Filter out tests that use f16/f80/f128/c_longdouble, @Vector, threadlocal, asm, u128 division or async.
- error_return_trace must be off.
- The default runner uses std.debug and an OS, so a custom runner is needed.
claims_to_verify: The custom-runner approach works for x86_64-freestanding (see the ziggit thread on freestanding testing)
How many behavior tests reference f16, f80, f128, c_longdouble, @Vector or threadlocal (grep test/behavior)
Test functions are reached by indirect call, so a test that returns an error can be reported without unwinding

picks.name: Zig lib/compiler_rt and its tests
picks.what: Zig's own compiler-rt written in Zig (__udivti3, __divti3, __fixdfti, float and int conversions, soft-float, __mulodi4 and so on) with in-file `test` blocks that call the helpers directly by name.
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 (direct calls to defined functions are ordinary calls, not legalizer libcalls)
picks.why_good: It covers exactly the helpers the backend defers to Phase 3, with exhaustive edge-case tests. Compiled to bitcode, it is also a candidate in-module implementation of those helpers for Phase 3 (an alternative to P/Invoke).
picks.blockers: Each helper's implementation must itself avoid the operation it implements (for example, udivmod written with u64 halves). The f80 and f128 helpers are out. Legalizer-generated helper calls are still reported as errors even though the definitions are present, so only the direct-call tests work in Phase 1.
claims_to_verify: compiler_rt's udivmod.zig and int.zig implement 128-bit division without emitting `udiv i128`
The tests build with the same custom runner and freestanding flags
Which compiler_rt files need f80/f128 or inline asm (exclude them)

picks.name: Zig std unit tests for OS-independent modules (std.math, std.hash, std.crypto, std.sort, std.unicode)
picks.what: The in-file test blocks of std modules that need no OS, run with the custom runner and a FixedBufferAllocator-backed testing allocator. std.crypto carries published vectors (SHA-2, BLAKE3, ChaCha20, Ed25519, AES software path).
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 for a subset. Phase 3 for anything using std.testing.allocator or page_allocator.
picks.why_good: Thousands of deterministic tests with built-in expectations. The crypto tests are vector-checked.
picks.blockers:
- std.testing.allocator may need an OS page allocator.
- std.fmt-based expectEqual messages use fmt (indirect calls, M9).
- Some crypto code selects x86 intrinsics by CPU feature, so -mcpu=baseline is needed.
claims_to_verify: `zig test lib/std/math.zig` (and the others) compiles for x86_64-freestanding with a custom runner
std.testing.allocator works freestanding or can be overridden
With -mcpu=baseline, std.crypto.aes takes the software path (no AES-NI)

languages.verdict: Good fit for computational kernels in Phase 1, and already verified: BLAS, the LAPACK DGESV chain and MINPACK all ran on .NET 8. Programs that use Fortran I/O, ALLOCATE or automatic arrays need flang-rt, so Phase 3. Fortran has no GC and no unwinding (STOP is a call). Prefer the windows-msvc triple: llvm.powi becomes a pow import there but the __powidf2 error on the Linux triple.
languages.integration_path: Stock flang 23.1.2: flang -c -emit-llvm -O2 --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc. Pass bitcode, not .ll, to the in-tree llc -mtriple=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc-msil, then ilasm and dotnet. For the Linux layout, use --target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu plus -fintrinsic-modules-path pointing at the windows-msvc finclude, and avoid real**integer. Phase 1 programs need: a driver written as `integer function main() bind(c,name='main')` that prints through bind(c) putchar/puts interfaces; the library and driver in one source (switch form with !dir$ fixed); and C or IR stubs for _FortranAProgramStart, _FortranAProgramEndStatement, _FortranAStopStatement and _FortranAStopStatementText. Phase 2: llvm-link or msil-ld archives. Phase 3: build flang-rt with the in-tree clang for the msil triple (AddFlangRT.cmake already uses -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti and -include stl-overrides.h) and link it in. pseudo-unit.cpp and the pseudo lock give a smaller intermediate step.
languages.earliest_phase: Phase 1 for kernels with a bind(c) driver and stubs. Phase 3 for ordinary PROGRAMs with I/O.
languages.blockers:
- main signature: flang emits `i32 @main(i32, ptr, ptr)` (verified at -O2). emitEntryPoint accepts only i32 main() or i32 main(i32, ptr), so every PROGRAM is rejected. Suggested fix: accept the 3-argument form and pass a null envp. Released Nim 2.x with --os:any, and GNAT front ends from GCC 16 or older, produce the same shape. Nim devel and current gcc master's gnatbind do not.
- Runtime entry points: every PROGRAM references _FortranAProgramStart and _FortranAProgramEndStatement. A stub written in Fortran with bind(c) crashed flang 23.1.2, so stubs must be C or IR.
- -O0 and -O1 leave llvm.stacksave and _FortranACharacterCompareScalar1 calls, so use -O2.
- BLOCK constructs keep stacksave/stackrestore at -O2 with no dynamic alloca (verified), and the fork rejects them. Suggested fix: make them no-ops when the function has no dynamic alloca.
- NINT becomes llvm.lround, which is reported as 'not a Phase-1 import' (verified). Define lround/lroundf in the module.
- real**integer becomes llvm.powi. That works on windows-msvc-msil (a pow import) but on linux-gnu-msil it is the __powidf2 Phase-3 error. integer**integer is inlined.
- Complex: ABS, EXP and SQRT call cabs, cexp and csqrt, which are not imports. Complex division calls __divdc3 (a Phase-3 helper error) unless -fcomplex-arithmetic=improved is used.
- Array-expression temporaries call malloc/free (Phase 3 or a module-local allocator). Automatic arrays become dynamic alloca (Phase 3).
- Internal procedures passed as actual arguments need trampolines, and the 'nest' parameter is rejected.
- REAL(16) is fp128, which is rejected.
- TLS and atomics: only flang-rt's pthread lock is affected (use the pseudo lock).

picks.name: Reference BLAS (Reference-LAPACK BLAS/SRC)
picks.what: Level 1/2/3 BLAS in S/D/C/Z precision with LSAME and a replaced XERBLA, driven by a bind(c) main that compares against exact integer-valued results.
picks.why_good: Already ran end to end (dgemm, dtrsm, idamax, zdotc, dnrm2, dznrm2) with exact expected values. It exercises complex results (sret on Windows, {double,double} on Linux), hidden CHARACTER lengths and assumed-size arrays.
picks.blockers: Replace XERBLA (it uses WRITE and STOP). Avoid complex ABS/SQRT/EXP and NINT in the driver.
claims_to_verify: The same module runs, not only compiles, on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-msil
-ffp-contract=off is needed for bit-exact comparison with a native build
flang output contains no GlobalAlias, since MSIL rejects every alias

picks.name: Reference LAPACK, solver subsets now, whole library in Phase 2
picks.what: Single-module subsets, growing to QR, Cholesky (recursive DPOTRF2), symmetric eigen and SVD drivers checked by residual identities. The DGESV chain is verified: 40x40 with 2 right-hand sides, max error below 1e-10, plus the XERBLA path.
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 for subsets. Phase 2 for the whole library as an archive or through LTO.
picks.why_good: Real numerical code with self-validating residual checks. It covers recursion, IEEECK's Inf/NaN arithmetic, DLAMCH intrinsics and ILAENV string logic.
picks.blockers: IPARMQ uses NINT, so define lroundf in the module. Driver array expressions call malloc. Whether routines outside the DGESV chain use automatic arrays is unchecked.
claims_to_verify: Which LAPACK routines use automatic arrays or BLOCK (dynamic alloca or stacksave)
The eigen and SVD drivers (DSYEV, DGESVD) hit no complex-division or powi helper
The residual thresholds that make tests deterministic across native and MSIL
The 2106-file count for SRC

picks.name: fortran-lang/minpack (modern MINPACK)
picks.what: HYBRD, HYBRJ, LMDIF, LMDER and LMSTR on standard problems (Rosenbrock and others), with the user function passed as a procedure dummy (a function pointer). src/minpack.f90 is 3832 lines, and test/ has six programs (test_chkder, test_hybrd, test_hybrj, test_lmder, test_lmdif, test_lmstr).
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 once stacksave/stackrestore without dynamic alloca become no-ops. Today it needs a bitcode edit.
picks.why_good: Verified after stripping stacksave: lmdif1 gave x=(1,1) with info=2, and hybrd1 gave 1.414213. It exercises callbacks through function pointers and BLOCK constructs.
picks.blockers:
- `main : block` brings stacksave.
- One `error stop` needs a StopStatementText stub.
- The C API passes an internal procedure, which needs trampolines (excluded).
- The test programs use formatted WRITE (Phase 3).
claims_to_verify: After the stacksave no-op change, minpack.f90 compiles unmodified
minpack.f90 has no automatic arrays (grep)
The six test programs could run in Phase 1 if their WRITEs go through a minimal stub

picks.name: TSVC (netlib vectord) and LINPACK (linpackd) kernels
picks.what: About 135 vectorizer-test loops with per-loop checksums (extracted from the shell archive with sed), plus the 100x100 LINPACK solve with its residual check. WRITE and second() are replaced by a putchar printer and a stub.
picks.why_good: Deterministic checksums. Large COMMON blocks become common-linkage globals. TSVC also has a C version in llvm-test-suite, so the same loops can be tested differentially through clang and flang.
picks.blockers:
- Formatted WRITE in check() and title() must be replaced.
- second() must be supplied.
- real**integer becomes llvm.powi: use the windows-msvc-msil triple (pow import), because linux-gnu-msil reports __powidf2.
- Look for NINT (lround).
claims_to_verify: The TSVC checksums match between flang-native and MSIL with -ffp-contract=off
The C TSVC in llvm-test-suite MultiSource/Benchmarks/TSVC covers the same loop set

picks.name: LLVM test-suite gfortran torture/execute (no-I/O subset)
picks.what: 225 small execute tests (223 .f90 + 2 .f) from GCC's gfortran torture suite. About 167 have no I/O or ALLOCATE, and their oracle is the exit status from STOP n or abort. DisabledFiles.cmake disables 8 (st_function, entry_2, specifics, data_3, getarg_1, intrinsic_sr_kind, nan_inf_fmt, random_2).
picks.earliest_phase: Phase 1 with the STOP stubs, plus either the 3-argument main fix or a rewrite that turns each program into a subroutine called by a bind(c) main. Phase 3 for the remaining ~58.
picks.why_good: Many small, focused language-feature tests with a trivial oracle. The Fortran counterpart of the C torture tests.
picks.blockers:
- The main signature and the ProgramStart/Stop stubs.
- Some tests may still hit array temporaries (malloc), NINT, descriptor intrinsics or complex helpers.
- Licensed GPL-3.0: fetch at test time rather than vendoring.
claims_to_verify: The 167/58 split by grep for I/O statements and ALLOCATE (the total of 225 is confirmed, the split was not re-derived)
How many of the 167 compile cleanly at -O2 with only the four stubs

picks.name: NIST FCVS (llvm-test-suite Fortran/UnitTests/fcvs21_f95)
picks.what: 180 FM*.f validation programs, each with a reference_output file, covering statements, intrinsics, formatted I/O, ASSIGN/GOTO and arithmetic IF.
picks.why_good: The standard F77 conformance suite. Outputs are deterministic, and llvm-test-suite already has the reference outputs and comparison options. It is the first real exercise of flang-rt on MSIL.
picks.blockers:
- flang-rt must be built for MSIL: P/Invoke libc, POSIX file calls, fenv in ProgramStart, and the pseudo lock or real locks.
- Some tests need -std=legacy.
- NO_STOP_MESSAGE handling.
claims_to_verify: flang-rt builds with the in-tree clang for the msil triple using the AddFlangRT.cmake flags
flang-rt's fenv calls (feclearexcept/fesetround) can be satisfied or stubbed under the CLR

languages.verdict: Good fit for Phase 1. BetterC drops druntime: no GC, TypeInfo, ModuleInfo, exceptions or module constructors. Structs with destructors, scope(exit), templates, CTFE and bounds-checked slices remain, which is IR shaped differently from C (destructor cleanups that would be landingpads with exceptions are plain code here).
languages.integration_path: ldc2 -betterC -mtriple=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -O2 -output-bc -checkaction=halt (flags verified in the LDC source). With -checkaction=halt, asserts and bounds failures become llvm.trap instead of a C assert call. Then llc -mtriple=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc-msil, ilasm and dotnet. Use extern(C) int main() and print through core.stdc putchar/puts. Use the MSVC triple, because `real` is x87 80-bit on x86 Linux and double under MSVC. LDC 1.43 supports LLVM 18-22 (prebuilt with 22.1.8), and its bitcode can be retargeted, which is easier than rebuilding LDC on LLVM 24.

- Unwinding: none under -betterC (no exceptions).
- GC: none under -betterC. Full druntime would need a conservative GC scanning the machine stack, which is never planned (LDC's wasm pointer-spill pass is a possible future model).

- Assert and bounds checks call the C runtime's assert unless -checkaction=halt is used (or the function is provided).
- printf is variadic (Phase 3).
- On Linux targets `real` is x86_fp80, which is rejected.

languages.verdict: Possible, but only with two TinyGo patches. Phase 1 needs -gc=leaking -scheduler=none -panic=trap on a custom target, plus disabling recover for that target (otherwise every function with defer gets an inline-asm setjmp-style checkpoint) and a runtime main that returns int32. A precise GC is plausible later through the stack-object root chain TinyGo already uses for wasm. Goroutines need assembly stack switching, so they are out.
languages.integration_path: tinygo build -o out.bc with a custom target JSON (llvm-target x86_64 Linux or Windows, gc leaking, scheduler none, a custom build tag), then the fork's llc -mtriple=...-msil. Patch compiler/defer.go so supportsRecover returns false for the target. Give the custom runtime its own exported main that returns int32, because runtime_unix.go's main returns Go int (i64). Provide a heap region (a static array exposed as the heap start and end symbols) and putchar. llvm.mem* intrinsics lower inline. TinyGo 0.42 builds with LLVM 22 (19 and 20 still work).
languages.earliest_phase: Phase 1 with the recover and main patches (leaking GC). A precise GC needs a further TinyGo patch.
languages.blockers:
- recover: TinyGo implements it with tinygo_longjmp and a per-architecture inline-asm checkpoint in every function with defer. supportsRecover is false only for wasm32 and xtensa. MSILPrepareIR rejects inline asm, so patch supportsRecover for an msil target.

- GC root finding: NeedsStackObjects is enabled only with the tinygo.wasm tag, so it would need an msil tag. That pass skips allocas, so address-taken locals in the localloc frame are not tracked.
- Panics exit once recover is disabled.
- Goroutines need -scheduler=tasks (assembly) or asyncify (wasm-only), so use none.
- Some runtime files are .S and need stubs.

With --mm:arc and --exceptions:goto, Nim exceptions compile to error flags checked after calls, with no unwinding and no setjmp, so even try/except works. Use --noMain with your own main, or --os:standalone (main(void), needs panicoverride), or Nim devel (2-argument main), or the backend's 3-argument fix. Compile the generated .c with the fork's clang for the msil triple, or with stock clang to bitcode plus llvm-link (one module in Phase 1), then run llc. A C shim provides malloc/free/realloc (a bump allocator), the panicoverride hooks and output. clang turns memcpy/memset calls into intrinsics, which lower inline.

- Allocator: -d:useMalloc needs malloc (a shim, or Phase 3).

Floating point is strictfp with constrained intrinsics unless fastmath is on; the fork lowers strict FP.

- Exceptions: invoke/landingpad with Itanium psABI EH (fpc_psabi_*), so never.

checks.subject: Standard ML (MLton)
checks.claim: MLton's LLVM codegen emits musttail between chunks, so musttail (rejected by the fork) blocks the -codegen llvm route
checks.correction: MLton emits musttail only when the Expert flag -chunk-tail-call true is set. Control.chunkTailCall defaults to false. By default, leaveChunk flushes the frontier and stackTop and returns nextBlock to a dispatcher, so it works like a trampoline and uses no musttail. Chunk functions use the default C calling convention. cc10 (the GHC convention, which the fork also rejects) appears only with -llvm-cc10 true, which also defaults to false. musttail is therefore not a default blocker.
checks.source: github.com/MLton/mlton master: mlton/codegen/llvm-codegen/llvm-codegen.fun (leaveChunk, ~line 1396); mlton/control/control-flags.sml (chunkTailCall default=false, llvmCC10 default=false); mlton/main/main.fun lines 300-302 and 602-603

checks.subject: Pascal (Free Pascal LLVM codegen)
checks.claim: try/except uses setjmp/longjmp, so it is a Phase 3 item
checks.correction: The LLVM backend uses invoke/landingpad with Itanium psABI exception handling (fpc_psabi_begin_catch, fpc_psabi_end_catch, resume). It does not use setjmp/longjmp. LowerInvoke removes this, so raising or catching a Pascal exception can never work: this is 'never', not Phase 3. The normal-path finally code is duplicated outside the landing pad, so try/finally without a raise still runs.
checks.source: FPC main compiler/llvm/llvmpi.pas (tllvmexceptionstatehandler: 'all calls inside the exception block have to be invokes', landingpad clauses, fpc_psabi_*); compiler/llvm/nllvmflw.pas

checks.subject: Pascal (Free Pascal LLVM codegen)
checks.claim: The Linux RTL makes syscalls that may be inline asm
checks.correction: This is stronger than a Phase 3 blocker. The default Linux RTL (without -dFPC_USE_LIBC) implements FpSysCall as x86_64 'assembler' routines. The LLVM backend emits assembler routines as naked functions containing inline asm ('call void asm sideeffect' in agllvm.pas). The fork rejects all inline asm and module asm (MSILPrepareIR.cpp line ~518, MSILAsmPrinter.cpp line ~380). An RTL rebuilt with FPC_USE_LIBC, or Pascal fallbacks, is a prerequisite.
checks.source: FPC rtl/linux/x86_64/syscall.inc; rtl/linux/Makefile.fpc (the FPC_USE_LIBC option); compiler/llvm/agllvm.pas (WriteFunctionFlags marks po_assembler routines naked); the fork's llvm/lib/Target/MSIL/MSILPrepareIR.cpp

checks.subject: Pascal (Free Pascal LLVM codegen)
checks.claim: ansistring refcounting may use atomic increment when multithreading is on
checks.correction: fpc_AnsiStr_Incr_Ref calls inclocked. On x86_64, inclocked is an assembler routine that tests IsMultithread and conditionally emits a LOCK prefix, so it is inline asm under the LLVM backend, not an LLVM atomic. The fork rejects it even in single-threaded programs. Also note that FPC marks functions strictfp and emits llvm.experimental.constrained.* for floating-point math unless fastmath is on. The fork does lower strict FP (LowerStrictFP).
checks.source: FPC rtl/inc/astrings.inc lines 137-142; rtl/x86_64/x86_64.inc line 1528 (inclocked assembler); rtl/inc/generic.inc (the non-atomic Pascal fallback is used only when FPC_SYSTEM_HAS_INCLOCKED_LONGINT is undefined); compiler/llvm/nllvmadd.pas
